reading.body:
Carrie Adams is disclosed as a lobbyist on three AI-related filings, all for one client, The AI Policy Network Inc., and all routed through a single lobbying firm.

The pattern is narrow and concentrated. Three filings, one client, one firm, but fourteen distinct bills named across them. That ratio is the useful detail: a small number of disclosure forms can carry a wide legislative footprint, because each filing names every bill the lobbyist touched. The prior government positions listed, spanning staff roles for two senators, a speaker, a committee, and two representatives, are what the Lobbying Disclosure Act requires filers to report from the prior twenty years. They are a disclosure requirement, not an inference about influence.

For AI specifically, this is the legislative layer rather than the compute layer. Nothing here concerns data centers, power, or chips. It shows which bills an AI-focused client was tracking in 2025 and later, and who was registered to carry that work. The bill numbers are listed without titles, subjects, or outcomes, so the data cannot say what any of them would do or whether they moved.

What it does not cover: the amounts paid, the specific agencies contacted, or any position taken on any bill. It also cannot distinguish routine registration from active advocacy. A separate lobbyist shares the name and has a separate record, so nothing here should be merged with that one.
